title: GUST: Graph Edge-Coloring Utilization for Accelerating Sparse Matrix Vector Multiplication
problem: Sparse matrix-vector multiplication (SpMV) suffers from poor hardware resource utilization on specialized accelerators due to irregular sparsity patterns. Traditional domain-specific architectures designed for SpMV or adapted from matrix-matrix multiplication accelerators cannot fully exploit hardware resources when processing sparse data.
motivation: SpMV is fundamental to scientific computing, engineering applications, and machine learning, making performance improvements critical for these domains.
method: GUST is a hardware/software co-design that separates multipliers and adders in the hardware architecture to enable resource sharing across multiple rows and columns. The design uses a specially devised edge-coloring scheduling algorithm to resolve collisions arising from resource sharing, improving overall hardware utilization and mitigating performance degradation from sparsity.
key_novelty: Separating multipliers and adders with graph-based edge-coloring scheduling to enable efficient resource sharing across multiple rows and columns for sparse matrix operations.
contributions: Novel hardware architecture with separated multipliers and adders enabling resource sharing across matrix rows and columns
Edge-coloring based scheduling algorithm to resolve collisions from resource sharing
Hardware/software co-design improving average hardware utilization to 33.67%
FPGA implementation achieving 411× speedup and 137× energy efficiency improvement over 1D systolic arrays

metrics.speedup: 411× vs length-256 1D systolic array, 108× vs length-87 1D systolic array
metrics.energy_or_tops_w: 137× energy efficiency improvement vs length-256 1D, 148× vs length-87 1D
metrics.other: 33.67% average hardware utilization; lower execution time on 7/9 matrices vs Serpens

limitations: Limitations not discussed in abstract; scalability, memory system impact, and collision handling complexity not addressed.
primary_theme: Sparse matrix acceleration through resource sharing
